meta.title: Kekal: a warranty that outlives the shop
meta.description: Kekal holds a shop's warranty money on Solana. If the shop stops answering a claim, the buyer is paid. If the shop goes silent, every holder is paid.
meta.ogAlt: Kekal: a warranty that outlives the shop. Three rules beside a sample warranty card showing a 25.00 kUSD reserve and a copper stamp marked Paid because the shop went silent.
home.lede: The shop's promise to install and service what it sold, backed by money it cannot take back while your warranty runs.

home.how.title: How it works
home.how.shop.title: The shop locks a reserve and prints a card
home.how.shop.body: For each sale the shop sets aside part of its deposit for that warranty and gives the buyer a printed card with a QR code. From then on the shop cannot take that money back until the warranty ends.
home.how.shop.alt: The shop board on a phone: card 0 issued, with its QR code and buttons to download it as PDF or PNG
home.how.card.title: The buyer scans the card and can claim
home.how.card.body: The QR code opens the warranty page. No wallet and no fees: the page shows the reserve held for the buyer, the deadline the shop must meet, and a form to file a claim.
home.how.card.alt: The buyer's warranty page on a phone: the deadline the shop must answer by, and the warranty card with the reserve held for the buyer
home.how.paid.title: The shop goes quiet, the buyer is paid
home.how.paid.body: If the shop lets the deadline pass, anyone can send the payout and the reserve moves to the card. Nobody has to approve it. If the shop answers and fixes the fault, nothing is paid and the warranty continues.
home.how.paid.alt: The no-wallet demo on a phone after the payout: the last steps with their public records and the card stamped Paid
home.how.note: Screens from the browser tests on an iPhone 13 screen, run on a local test validator.

home.why.title: Why
home.why.promise: A shop that installs solar panels, air conditioners or water heaters gives two promises. The maker's warranty covers the unit. The shop's own promise covers the work: installing it properly and coming back when something fails.
home.why.insurance: The second promise lasts only as long as the shop does. In the United Kingdom, certified solar installers must insure that promise so it is still honoured if the company stops trading.
home.why.program: Kekal does that job with a program instead of an insurer: the money behind the promise sits where the shop cannot take it back, and anyone can check it.
home.why.origin: It was built in Malaysia by a developer who writes software for a small solar business, where every quotation carries a printed warranty certificate.
home.faq.title: Questions
home.faq.lock.q: Why would a shop lock money?
home.faq.lock.a: Because a backed warranty is easier to sell. The reserve is small per sale and comes back when the warranty ends. No shop has used Kekal yet.
home.faq.arbiter.q: Who is the arbiter, and what if they side with the shop?
home.faq.arbiter.a: The shop names the arbiter when it opens, and the buyer can see who it is. The program limits the role: the arbiter rules only on disputed claims, cannot be the shop's own key, and if it does not rule in time the buyer is paid. A neutral panel is not built.
home.faq.database.q: Why not a database or an insurer?
home.faq.database.a: A database lives with whoever runs it, and the reserve has to outlive the shop. An insurer needs a company behind it; a program does not, and anyone can check the reserve.
home.faq.stablecoin.q: The buyer is paid in a stablecoin. What can they do with it?
home.faq.stablecoin.a: It lands on the card's key and can be sent to any Solana address. Cashing out to ringgit is not built. Only the shop has to hold crypto.
home.faq.heartbeat.q: What if the shop forgets to check in?
home.faq.heartbeat.a: The shop chooses its check-in window and a grace period when it opens, and any action the owner takes counts as a check-in. Past both, the buyers are paid. That is the promise.
home.faq.code.a: AI coding agents wrote the program, the web app, the tests and this page. The author ran them, checked the results with separate review sessions and is responsible for the project. The AI usage notes in the source code list what was checked and the limits of that review.
home.limits.title: Limits
home.limits.devnet: Test network only. The program has not been audited. Do not use it with real money.
home.limits.cashout: No cash-out to ringgit. A paid buyer receives a stablecoin on a key; turning it into ringgit is outside the program.
home.limits.arbiter: The arbiter is trusted. The shop names it or takes the default one. The program only makes sure the arbiter is not the shop owner and that an arbiter who does nothing still loses to the deadline.
home.limits.admin: The first caller of the setup step becomes the admin. It is not yet tied to the program's upgrade key; the deploy script calls it right after the deploy and stops unless the deploy key is the admin.
home.limits.keeper: Someone has to send the settling transactions. No signature from the shop or the buyer is needed, but if no keeper or person sends them, the money waits until someone does.
home.limits.capital: The shop must hold a stablecoin and lock capital. That is a real cost for a small shop, and the reserve per sale is the shop's decision.
home.limits.bearer: The QR card is a bearer key. Whoever holds the card can claim. A lost card can be moved to a new key only while the old one is still at hand.
